topics.text:
I was trying to solve this problem, ProblemThe number 40,231 is a five-digit positive integer that uses five consecutive digits, although not necessarily in order. How many such five-digit numbers are

there?
. The official solution was: Sol$696$
, but I kept getting $600$.



My Solution:

My SolWe can use constructive counting to solve this problem. Since the maximum digit, is $9$, the minimum digit can range from $1$ to $5$, leaving $5$ options. Then, there is $5$ factorial, or $120$ ways, to arrange the digits, of that number. $5\times 5! = 600$. What did I do wrong?

topics.title: Don't Understand
topics.text:
2016 AMC 10A



The solution from the AoPS Wiki says



[quote = AoPS Wiki]By Hockey Stick Identity, the number of terms that have all $a,b,c,d$ raised to a positive power is $\binom{N-1}{3}+\binom{N-2}{3}+\cdots + \binom{4}{3}+\binom{3}{3}=\binom{N}{4}$. We now want to find some $N$ such that $\binom{N}{4} = 1001$. As mentioned above, after noticing that $1001 = 7\cdot11\cdot13$, and some trial and error, we find that $\binom{14}{4} = 1001$, giving us our answer of $N=\boxed{14}$[/quote]



My question is, how did they get that expression for the number of terms that all have $a, b, c, d$ raised to a positive power? Doesn't make sense to me. If we use the Binomial Theorem and treat it like

$((a+ b+c+d) + 1)^N$ couldn't we say $\binom{N}{0} + \binom{N}{1} + \cdots + \binom{N}{N-1}$ as the number of terms there are with a, b, c, and d all raised to a positive power?



Thanks!



I'm not sure if this is the right place to put it, either here or C&P...?

topics.title: k My MATHCOUNTS Journey So Far... (inspired by fatant)
topics.text:
So, after reading fatant's "My Experience with MATHCOUNTS", I decided to share what MATHCOUNTS has been like for me so far (I'm in 7th grade, so I have another go at Nationals).

Grade 6:The previous year, my math teacher had recommended me for MATHCOUNTS. I got a 14 on the 2014 AMC 8 (rip me) but managed to ace the 2014-15 Division E MOEMS without even trying (that competition was really easy for me...)

But now, it was 6th grade! I signed up for MATHCOUNTS, along with my old friend Aditya11 (after a point, the two of us dominated the club), hoping to beast everyone.



School Competition, December 18, 2015:Right before the Sprint Round, the teachers showed us that clip where Yoda goes, "For my ally is the Force..." (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HMUKGTkiWik), and Aditya and I sat together (of course) as the competition began.



Sprint was not as good as I would have hoped, and I bombed Target: My overall score was 29 (19 Sprint, 10 Target), yet SOMEHOW I still make the third round of Countdown (top 16; I was 9th  :( rip), placing 4th in my school! (Our School Competition is done with a few other local schools...)



So, a crappy score made the school team for Chapter only by a miracle....


Chapter Competition, February 6, 2016:From my Middle School (of absolute suckiness), I rode a friend's car to the Coast Guard Academy, the site of our Chapter Competition. Once we got there, they had a whole [    ]-ton of donuts (I think I only took 2, because, besides, I wasn't all that hungry, having eaten breakfast at home already). We went into a big lecture hall and took our seats. First came the Sprint Round... I still can't believe I got this problem wrong:

[quote="2016 MATHCOUNTS Chapter Sprint"]9. A rectangular piece of paper measures 40 inches on its long side. It is folded in half along the dotted line. The ratio of the long side of the original sheet to the short side of the original sheet is the same as the ratio of the long side of the folded sheet to the short side of the folded sheet. What is the length of the short side of the original sheet? Express your answer in simplest radical form.[/quote]

Now, isn't that easy? You just write it out as a proportion and solve: $\frac{40}{x}$ = $\frac{x}{20}$ -> $x$ = $20$$\sqrt{2}$

I got at least 4 right on Target (I know, I sucked...  :( rip) and bombed Team, only getting 3 right (HOW???).

Then came lunch, which was pizza. I took a slice or two, then just went hanging around until... what... 1:00?

And then this random dude from the Mystic Aquarium comes and gives a really bad presentation (god, do you know your grammar?) It was so bad that the title was literally "How to use math in Ocean Sciences?"

I mean, WHAT SORT OF PROFESSIONALISM DOES THAT DEMONSTRATE??!?!

I got 20th overall (1st in my school, which really sucks) and watched the Countdown Round... this OP kid behind me got like every single question right.

Afterward, I found that I made States! (but not Aditya11... rip)


State Competition, March 12, 2016:The day had come... nothing much else to say... but...

who else thought that the 2016 States were harder than usual? (RIP SPRINT #30)

Needless to say, I got 63rd (2nd in my school)... rip  :(


SCORES/RANKINGS:

SCHOOL: 29 (19 Sp, 5 Ta)/4th

CHAPTER: ?/20th

STATE: 20 (12 Sp, 4 Ta)/63rd

Advanced to Nationals: no  :( rip


Grade 7:School Competition, December 20, 2016:THIS time around, we were ready to beast! With another OP kid (MasonG314) by our side, we were looking to dominate our school in the school round. And so... it began. Sprint was way too easy (I aced it!), and I only missed the last question on Target (the answer was 38? how?). I ended up getting an easy 1st with a score of 44, BUT THEN some 8th grader beat me in CD.


Chapter Competition, February 4, 2017:Much like last year, except that I did absolutely beast, getting 27 on Sprint and 6 on Target, giving me a total score of 39 (1 point behind Aditya11 :furious: ). Well, then again, that was partially because this year's Chapter round was EASY AF... In any case, I made CD and swept everyone, getting 1st. I was also part of the 1st-place team, and 4th overall.


State Competition, March 11, 2017:The day had come. After a month of intense grinding with Aditya11, it was time to prove our skills to the state. We went into the room, chatting a bit with fellow AoPSers franchester and ProGameXD, before the competition began. Sprint was quite hard this time around; I only managed to get 16 right... No. 21 was so easy... Now, don't tell anyone this, but I've seen No. 7 on Target before. Overall, Target was easier than I expected! I got 12th overall, and 10th in team. In CD, I made it to the 2nd round but then got 2-1ed by this other OP kid...




SCORES/RANKINGS:

SCHOOL: 44 (30 Sp, 7 Ta)/1st

CHAPTER: 39 (27 Sp, 6 Ta)/4th

STATE: 28 (16 Sp, 6 Ta)/12th

Advanced to Nationals: no  :( rip


Me now...For the past few months, I've been going on full rage-trigger mode, and I plan to spam (pirated) National tests over the summer, as well as taking the AoPS class MATHCOUNTS/AMC 8 Advanced...

I WILL MAKE NATS IN 8TH GRADE, PEOPLE. MARK MY WORDS!


TO BE CONTINUED...

topics.title: k Modular Arithmetic: A Problem of Modular Equidistribution
topics.text:
Hi Everyone,

So I was wondering whether or not the elements of the set of all integers $\mathbb{Z}$, when considered in modulo $n$ are uniformly distributed for all values of $k\pmod{n}$. For example, this works when considering the total number of three digit integers congruent to $12\pmod{60}$. Writing out the inequality in the form $12+60t$ and solving for the interval of valid values of $t$, gives that there are exactly 15 integers congruent to $12\pmod{60}$. However, let's try to solve this same problem by assuming that these integers are uniformly distributed in $\pmod{60}$. Another way of looking at this is that there are an equal number of integers in each of the $60$ modular residue classes $k\pmod{60}$, where $k\in [0,59] \cap \mathbb{Z}$. Assuming this yields a $1/60$ probability that a three digit integer is congruent to $12\pmod{60}$. Moreover, using the Fundamental Counting Principle yields a total of $9 \cdot 10 \cdot 10=900$ three digit integers. Therefore, multiplying the probability of $1/60$ by the total number of three digit integers ($900$) gives $900/60=15$. In this case my conjecture works. But does it work in general, why or why not. Please explain.



Thanks,

Mathchampion1

topics.title: Evaluate Large Factorials
topics.text:
The Problem

A friend of mine, theorized a probability question: Suppose a box has $7,000$ red balls, $5,000$ green balls, and $2,000$ white balls. What is the probability that $7,000$ people grab the $7,000$ white balls, consecutively (right after each other). The balls are not placed back into the box.



This problem seems quite trivial; simply $\frac{7000}{14000}*\frac{6999}{13999}$ until $\frac{1}{7000}$. This can be written as: $\frac{7000!}{14000p6999}$.



The Issue:

However, a simple question arise: how does one go about, solving a large factorial, such as $7000!$?
